title: Integrating Generative AI Tools into Cloud Native Applications
overview: Connect the Transformer’s attention mechanism to practical uses of language models. Compare a plain model call, retrieval-augmented generation and tool-using agents, then place them in the GenAI stack. Choose the simplest pattern that supplies the context or actions the application needs, with a clear business benefit.
big_ideas: Transformers enable parallel computation over training inputs with self-attention; autoregressive generation still produces tokens sequentially.
Self-attention uses Query, Key and Value vectors: compare a word's Query with every Key, softmax the scores into weights, and sum the weighted Values.
A plain LLM uses supplied context; RAG adds retrieved information; an agent selects steps or tools and can also use RAG.
An agent sits at the centre, using one or more LLMs plus integrations (tools, vector store, prompt recipes); frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex help build it.
Generative model families: encoder models (VAE), GANs, autoregressive, flow, energy-based and diffusion models.
Foundation models are pre-trained once on massive data (high cost, high performance) and then adapted by fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
GenAI tech stack: hardware, cloud platforms, foundation models, customisation, then end-to-end applications.
Business value: creativity, personalisation, faster answers, simplifying complex systems, automating admin, content at scale.

sections.title: From RNNs to Transformers
sections.summary: The short history that led to Transformers, contrasting the sequential RNN with the parallel, attention-based Transformer.

notes.lead: Transformers improve training parallelism and context handling.
items: **Self-attention** → **connects positions directly**; allows **parallel computation** over **known training inputs**
**Autoregressive Transformer** → still **generates its output token by token**
notes.foot: **Parallel training** does **not** mean all **future output tokens** are known at once.

items: **Self-attention** → a position **combines allowed context positions directly**
**2017 paper** → **Attention Is All You Need** introduced the **Transformer**
**Not a claim** that one vendor's model **descended from** another vendor's product

terms.def: Recurrent Neural Network: processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying state forward.
Neural network architecture (2017) that processes sequences in parallel using self-attention.
Generative Pretrained Transformer, the model family behind ChatGPT.

check.q: A team training a language model on a large corpus finds an RNN takes weeks because each step waits for the previous one. Why would a Transformer train faster on the same hardware?

items: **RNN**: passes context through **recurrent state** one step at a time → training can't be **parallelised** across a sequence
**Self-attention**: connects positions directly → computation over the **known training input** can run **in parallel**, which suits **GPU** hardware
**Long-range links**: also links **distant words** without passing through every step in between

check.q: A colleague says 'Transformers process everything in parallel, so a chatbot built on one generates its whole answer at once'. Is that right?

a.lead: **No.** Parallelism applies to **training** over known inputs.
items: **Autoregressive** Transformer (such as a **GPT-style** model) still generates output **token by token**
Each new token **predicted from the context so far**
→ **streaming** the output token by token is common in chat applications

visuals.title: RNN vs Transformer
rows: Steps one after another; state carried from time step to time step
Parallel over known input positions; output generation remains autoregressive
Context travels through the recurrent state
Self-attention captures context and long-distance connections

sections.title: How self-attention works
sections.summary: Self-attention explained with a library analogy (Query, Key, Value) and a four-step computation giving each word a context-rich representation.

notes.lead: Each word builds its meaning from the words that matter most to it. Analogy:
items: **Keys** → the **labels** of every other word you **match against**
**Values** → the **content you collect** from the **best matches**
**Form learned Query, Key and Value vectors**
notes.foot: Lecture illustration: **'it'** attends more to **'animal'** than **'street'**. The numbers are **explanatory examples**, not **fixed learned rules**.

items: **Encoder-decoder models** → also use **cross-attention** to connect **decoder queries** with **encoder outputs**

terms.def: Mechanism combining Value vectors using Query–Key relevance weights over allowed context positions.
Three learned vectors per word: the question, the label to match against, and the content to take.
Function that turns raw scores into weights that add up to 1.

check.q: In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', explain how self-attention gives 'it' the right meaning, and what would change in 'because it was too wide'.

items: **Query** for 'it' is scored against every word's **Key**
**Weighted sum of Values** → 'it' gets a representation built mostly from **'animal'**
**'because it was too wide'**: the context changes the scores → **'street'** would get the higher weight
a.foot: The weights are **learned from data**, not fixed rules.

check.q: What would go wrong if the attention scores were used directly as weights, without softmax?

items: **Raw scores**: on an **arbitrary scale** and can be **negative**
→ the weighted sum of Values would not be a **proper average**; could be dominated by **scale rather than relevance**
**Softmax**: turns the scores into **positive weights that sum to 1** → output is a **weighted average** that favours the best-matching words

check.q: A text-generation model must not use words that come later in the sentence when predicting the next word, but a translation model's encoder can read the whole source sentence. How does attention differ between them?

items: **Generating decoder**: **causal attention** → **masks future positions**, so each token attends only to earlier ones
**Encoder-decoder** models: also **cross-attention** → the decoder's **queries** can look at the **encoder's outputs**

steps.label: Create Q, K, V
steps.detail: Query = question, Key = label, Value = content.

steps.label: Score
steps.detail: Score this token’s Query against context Keys, respecting any mask that excludes future positions.

steps.label: Softmax
steps.detail: Weights sum to 1; e.g. 'it' gives 0.8 to 'animal', 0.05 to 'street'.

steps.label: Weighted sum
steps.detail: Result is a context-rich representation of the word.

sections.title: LLM vs RAG vs Agents, and what GenAI is
sections.summary: Three ways of using a language model (plain LLM, RAG, agent), the parts of an autonomous agent, and a definition of Generative AI.

notes.lead: Choose by missing information or action.
items: **Plain LLM** → **learned parameters** plus the supplied **prompt/context**; does **not inherently fetch current company data**
**RAG** → **retrieves documents** and **adds them to that context**
**Agent** → can **select tools** and **act over several steps**, often also using **retrieval**
notes.foot: These patterns **combine**; they are **not a compulsory ladder**.

items: **Persistent vector memory** is **not required** for every **tool-using agent**
**Generative AI** → the part of **machine learning** that **learns the patterns and distribution** of a **training dataset** and **samples new, similar content** from it

terms.def: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant context and give it to the LLM with the prompt.
An LLM-centred system that selects steps or tools to pursue a task; it can use retrieval and memory where needed.
Database of embeddings used to find semantically similar content for context and memory.
Orchestration frameworks for wiring LLMs to data, memory and tools.

check.q: An HR chatbot built on a plain LLM call gives confident but outdated answers about this year's leave policy. Which pattern fixes this, and why not retrain the model?

items: **RAG**: retrieve the **current policy documents** and add them to the **prompt** → answers **grounded** in the company's own, **up-to-date** data
**Plain LLM**: only knows its **training data** plus the prompt
**Retraining**: **costly** and goes **stale** again with the next policy change; updating the **document index** is cheap
a.foot: Keep the index current, because RAG is **only as fresh as its sources**.

check.q: A RAG assistant retrieves the refund policy correctly. The business now wants it to issue refunds as well. What changes in the design, and what new risk appears?

items: **Tool selection**: the model selects tools, such as calling the **order and payment service APIs**
**Multi-step**: acts over several steps, still using **retrieval** for policy
**New risk**: retrieval gave the model **information, not permission**
**Safeguards**: each tool needs **authorisation checks**, **limits** such as a **refund cap**, and **logging**, with **human approval** for high-value actions

check.q: A team building an agent that calls two internal APIs says it must first set up a vector store for memory. Is that required?

items: **Lecture's agent architecture**: an **interface**, a **model**, **instructions** or a **prompt recipe**, **planning**, **tool integrations**, **memory or context**
**Tool-using agent with short tasks**: may need only **conversation context**
**Add a vector store** when the agent must retrieve from a **large document set**

check.q: A RAG assistant cites a company document but still gives a wrong answer. Give two likely causes and how you would confirm each.

items: **Stale or irrelevant passage** retrieved → confirm: check the **retrieved chunks** and their **dates**
**Model misread correct context** → confirm: check whether the answer is actually **supported by the retrieved text**
a.foot: Retrieval is **not a correctness guarantee**, so evaluate **retrieval quality** and **answer support** separately.

steps.label: User question
steps.detail: Define the information need; the model does not automatically know private or current documents.

steps.label: Retrieve passages
steps.detail: Find context in an appropriate authorised source; retrieval quality limits what evidence is available.

steps.label: Assemble prompt
steps.detail: Supply selected passages alongside the question. This changes context without changing model weights.

steps.label: Generate answer
steps.detail: The LLM uses the prompt and its learned patterns. Check that the answer is actually supported; retrieval alone does not guarantee correctness.

sections.title: Model families, value and the GenAI stack
sections.summary: Six families of generative models, why businesses want GenAI services, and foundation models with the layered GenAI tech stack.

items: **Autoregressive models** → **predict the next value** from previous ones (how **LLMs write text**)
**Energy-based models** → **low energy to real data**, **high to others**
**Diffusion models** → learn to **reverse** a defined **noise-adding process**
notes.foot: **GAN vs diffusion**: **adversarial competition** vs **reversing gradual noising**.

items: **Pre-trained once**, at **high cost**, on **massive broad data**
**Foundation models** → **closed via API**, or **open-weight** with **released parameters**
**Closed** → **ready to use** but **ties you to a provider**
**Released weights** → can allow **self-hosting** and **tuning** under their **licence**

terms.def: Generative Adversarial Network: a generator and discriminator trained against each other.
Learns to reverse a noise-adding process, generating data by gradually denoising.
Large model pre-trained on massive broad data, adapted to many downstream tasks.
Platform to share and host models, e.g. Hugging Face.
Further training a pre-trained model on domain data to specialise it.

check.q: A design team wants a model that generates realistic product images, and is comparing a GAN with a diffusion model. Explain how each generates, as the basis for the comparison.

sub: Trains a **generator** against a **discriminator** that tries to tell real images from generated ones
Generates in **one pass** from the trained generator
Generates by **progressively denoising** a random sample over **many steps**

check.q: A hospital must keep patient text inside its own environment, but wants to summarise clinical notes with a language model. Closed model through an API, or open-weight model self-hosted?

a.lead: **Open-weight model, self-hosted** in the hospital's environment.
items: **Fits the data constraint**: the **released weights** allow deployment and **tuning** under their **licence** without sending notes to a provider
**Closed API**: ready to use but **ties you to the provider** and sends data **outside**
a.foot: A closed API fits only if its **terms** and **deployment options** meet the constraint.

check.q: A startup plans to train its own foundation model for customer-support answers. What does the GenAI stack suggest instead?

a.lead: Most teams add value **higher up the stack**.
items: **Foundation models**: **expensive to pre-train** but **reusable** across many tasks
a.foot: Training their own model is justified only for a **capability** or a **data constraint** that existing models can't meet.

layers.label: End-to-end applications
layers.detail: User-facing apps with proprietary AI models (e.g. Midjourney, Runway, ActiveChat.AI).

layers.label: Customisation
layers.detail: Fine-tuning, prompt engineering and adaptation for domain-specific use cases.

layers.label: Foundation models
layers.detail: Broadly pretrained models can be consumed through an API or deployed from released weights where permitted. Weight availability and open-source licensing are separate questions.

layers.label: Cloud platforms
layers.detail: Google Cloud, AWS, Azure (also CoreWeave): scalable compute, storage and AI services over virtualised infrastructure.

layers.label: Hardware
layers.detail: GPUs, TPUs, servers and accelerator chips for AI training and inference.

sections.title: Key applications and use cases
sections.summary: GenAI application areas, with concrete business use cases for voice, video, text and music generation.

notes.foot: For an **architect** each is a **capability consumed as a service through APIs**.

items: **AI phone agents and IVR** → **cut wait times**
**Brand jingles**, **adaptive soundtracks**, **ad tracks** → where the applicable **usage terms permit**

terms.def: Interactive Voice Response: automated phone menu systems.

check.q: A bank wants to cut call-centre wait times with GenAI. Which application fits, and what must be added for it to be accurate?

a.lead: An **AI phone agent**: **speech interaction** + a **language-model service** that handles **routine enquiries**.
items: **Accuracy**: answers must come from **maintained knowledge sources** (**RAG**)
**Handoff to a human** for complex or sensitive cases

check.q: A marketing team wants lip-synced localised versions of a training video in 12 languages, plus a brand jingle. What does the architect need to check before treating these as simple API calls?

a.lead: Each capability can be consumed as a **service through APIs**, but check:
items: **Quality review for each language**: **translation** and **lip-sync errors** are public
**Usage and licence terms** for generated **voice**, **likeness** and **music**
**Human approval step** in the workflow before **publication**

exam_angles.q: Design a GenAI customer-support assistant for a cloud-native e-commerce platform that must answer from current product and policy documents and also check order status. Choose plain LLM, RAG or agent, and say how it fits into the existing microservices.

a.lead: **RAG** for answers, extended to an **agent** for order status.
items: **RAG**: retrieve current **product docs**, **FAQs** and **policies** from an index such as a **vector store** → responses **grounded** without retraining
**Agent tools**: **order status** by calling the **order service's existing API** with the **customer's own authorisation**
**Fit with microservices**: run the assistant as **its own service** behind the **API gateway**, using a **hosted foundation model** through an API or a **self-hosted open-weight** model

exam_angles.q: Explain the layers of the GenAI tech stack, and advise a 10-person cloud-native team on where to invest and where to buy.

sub: Where the team's **data** and **domain knowledge** create value

a.foot: Choose **closed versus open weights** by **data constraints** and **operating capacity**.

exam_angles.q: An enterprise wants GenAI for expense processing: answer staff questions about the policy, read receipt images and submit claims. Compare a plain LLM, RAG and an agent for this, and design the safeguards for the part that acts.

items: **Plain LLM**: can interpret text but doesn't know the company's **current policy**
**RAG**: adds the **retrieved policy** → enough for **staff questions**
**Agent** with **tools** calling the **expense system's API**: needed for **extracting receipt data** and **submitting claims**

sub: Tools act only with the **employee's permissions**
**Limits** route claims above a **threshold** to **human approval**
Agent can only **prepare or submit** within **defined integrations**

a.foot: The patterns **combine**, but **an answer is not a permitted business action**.

exam_angles.q: A product manager asks why chat responses get slower as answers get longer, even though 'Transformers are parallel'. Explain using the RNN-to-Transformer change, and give one design implication for a cloud-native chat service.

items: **Training**: runs **in parallel** over known inputs and links **distant context** directly → made **large-scale training** possible
**Generation**: still **autoregressive**; each token predicted from the tokens so far → a **longer answer takes longer** to generate
**Design implication**: **stream tokens** to the client as they are generated; set **timeouts** and **capacity** by **expected output length**

exam_angles.q: A global marketing organisation proposes three GenAI features: personalised video per customer segment, first-draft product copy in 8 languages, and AI-generated ad music. Assess each for business value and risk, and say what process control is needed across all three.

sub: Risk: **costliest** to generate; most **likeness** and **brand risk**
Risk: its **usage terms** must permit **commercial use**

a.foot: **Process control** across all three: **human review and approval** before **publication**, and **track the usage terms** of each generated asset.
